lead: State-space analysis describes a system by first-order equations for its internal variables, not only by input-output transfer functions. After this unit you can build state models, solve them in time, test controllability and observability, and place closed-loop poles by state feedback.
about: The unit starts in 6.1 with the meaning of state and the general model x' = Ax + Bu, y = Cx + Du. 6.2 converts transfer functions into canonical state models and back. 6.3 solves the state equation using the matrix exponential and the state transition matrix. 6.4 tests whether inputs can move every state and whether outputs reveal every state. 6.5 uses those tests to design state feedback and place poles. The chapters build in that order: model, convert, solve, test, design. Worked examples use 2×2 systems so the matrix arithmetic stays on one phone screen.

chapters.idea: A system's future depends on a finite set of present variables called the state, and the state model writes the dynamics as first-order matrix equations.
chapters.depth: Define state, state variables, state vector and state model. Give general form x' = Ax + Bu, y = Cx + Du with sizes A (n×n), B (n×m), C (p×n), D (p×m). Show the integrator realization. Build a state model from a differential equation by choosing phase variables x1 = y, x2 = y', and so on. Some syllabi call this 'state variable analysis' or 'state-space representation'. Some syllabi apply the same model to physiological systems such as lung mechanics and blood glucose regulation; treat these as examples, not new theory.

figure.title: State model
figure.aria: Input u passes through B into a sum, then an integrator produces x; x goes through C to y and back through A to the sum.

chapters.example: A system obeys y'' + 5y' + 6y = 2u. With x1 = y and x2 = y', find A, B, C, D for output y. Answer: A = [[0, 1], [−6, −5]], B = [0; 2], C = [1, 0], D = 0.
chapters.trap: State variables are not unique; many state vectors describe the same system, so do not expect one fixed answer. Also check the sign of coefficients in A and the size of B.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 differential equations and transfer functions.
chapters.leave: Block diagram reduction and signal flow graphs stay in Unit 1.

chapters.idea: A transfer function can be written as a state model in canonical form, and a state model can be converted back to a transfer function.
chapters.depth: Convert G(s) = N(s)/D(s) to controllable canonical form (also called phase variable or companion form), observable canonical form and diagonal form for distinct poles. Write the state equation back as G(s) = C(sI − A)<sup>−1</sup>B + D. Handle strictly proper and proper cases; D is nonzero when numerator and denominator degrees are equal. Only a few universities teach Jordan form for repeated poles; keep that part short.

figure.aria: A transfer function splits into controllable, observable and diagonal state-model forms.

chapters.example: G(s) = (2s + 3)/(s² + 5s + 6). Write a controllable canonical state model and recover G(s) from it. Answer: A = [[0, 1], [−6, −5]], B = [0; 1], C = [3, 2], D = 0; C(sI − A)<sup>−1</sup>B = (2s + 3)/(s² + 5s + 6).
chapters.trap: In controllable canonical form the last row of A carries −a0, −a1 with signs. C carries numerator coefficients in ascending order; mixing ascending and descending order is the usual error.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.1; Unit 1 transfer functions; Unit 3 characteristic equation.
chapters.leave: Similarity transformations and Jordan form for repeated poles are advanced; leave them to a later course.

chapters.idea: The state equation has a closed-form solution built from the matrix exponential, which is the state transition matrix.
chapters.depth: Solve x' = Ax + Bu with initial state x(0). Zero-input solution is Φ(t)x(0). Zero-state solution is the convolution ∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup> Φ(t − τ)Bu(τ)dτ. State transition matrix Φ(t) = e<sup>At</sup> = L<sup>−1</sup>[(sI − A)<sup>−1</sup>]. List properties Φ(0) = I, Φ(t1 + t2) = Φ(t1)Φ(t2), Φ<sup>−1</sup>(t) = Φ(−t). Compute 2×2 cases by Laplace or eigenvalues. Only a few universities teach the Cayley-Hamilton series method in detail.

figure.title: State solution
figure.aria: The state equation is transformed to find Φ(t); the response sums the initial-state term and the input convolution.

chapters.example: For A = [[0, 1], [−2, −3]], find Φ(t). Then find x(t) for u = 0 and x(0) = [1; 0]. Answer: Φ(t) = [[2e<sup>−t</sup> − e<sup>−2t</sup>, e<sup>−t</sup> − e<sup>−2t</sup>], [−2e<sup>−t</sup> + 2e<sup>−2t</sup>, −e<sup>−t</sup> + 2e<sup>−2t</sup>]], and x(t) = [2e<sup>−t</sup> − e<sup>−2t</sup>; −2e<sup>−t</sup> + 2e<sup>−2t</sup>].
chapters.trap: Do not exponentiate A element by element. e<sup>At</sup> is a matrix; compute (sI − A)<sup>−1</sup> or use eigenvalues.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.1; Laplace transforms; Unit 2 time response.
chapters.leave: Laplace transform tables come from mathematics; do not re-derive them here.

chapters.idea: Controllability asks whether the input can move every state; observability asks whether the output can reveal every initial state.
chapters.depth: Define controllability and observability for linear time-invariant systems. Rank tests: Qc = [B AB ... A<sup>n−1</sup>B] must have rank n; Qo = [C; CA; ...; CA<sup>n−1</sup>] must have rank n. Mention the PBH test with eigenvalues; only a few universities teach PBH in detail. State the duality: (A, B) controllable iff (A<sup>T</sup>, B<sup>T</sup>) observable. Show that a stable system can still be uncontrollable.

figure.aria: Input u enters state x2; x1 feeds the output y, and the two states are coupled.

chapters.example: For A = [[0, 1], [−2, −3]], B = [0; 1], C = [1, 0], test controllability and observability. Answer: Qc = [B AB] = [[0, 1], [1, −3]], det = −1, rank 2, controllable. Qo = [C; CA] = [[1, 0], [0, 1]], det = 1, rank 2, observable.
chapters.trap: Use n columns for Qc and n rows for Qo, not just one. A system can be stable but uncontrollable, so stability does not imply controllability.
chapters.leave: Minimal realization and Kalman decomposition are advanced; leave them to a later course.

chapters.idea: If a system is controllable, state feedback can move its closed-loop poles to chosen positions.
chapters.depth: Use u = r − Kx. Closed-loop model x' = (A − BK)x + Br. Choose K by matching the characteristic polynomial of A − BK to the desired polynomial. For single-input systems, Ackermann's formula K = [0 ... 0 1] Qc<sup>−1</sup> φ(A); only a few universities require Ackermann, polynomial matching is enough for 2×2. Check controllability before placement. P, PI and PID controllers are in Unit 5; here K is a full state-feedback matrix, not one PID gain.

figure.title: State feedback
figure.aria: The gain K feeds every state back to the summing junction; the closed-loop matrix is A − BK.

chapters.example: A = [[0, 1], [0, 0]], B = [0; 1]. Place the closed-loop poles at −2 and −3 using u = r − Kx. Answer: desired (s + 2)(s + 3) = s² + 5s + 6; A − BK = [[0, 1], [−k1, −k2]], so k1 = 6, k2 = 5, K = [6 5].
chapters.trap: With u = r − Kx the closed-loop matrix is A − BK. Using u = r + Kx changes the signs of K. Always test controllability before placing poles.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.4 controllability; Unit 3 pole locations; Unit 5 controllers for P/PI/PID context.
chapters.leave: Observer design and LQR are advanced; LQR belongs to Unit 7.
